prompt: Why does a long context cost GPU memory?
answer_markdown: Because the KV cache stores a key and a value vector for every token, at every layer, and it lives in the same VRAM as the model weights. Its size is layers times heads times head_dim times 2 (for K and V) times bytes per value times sequence length times batch size — linear in sequence length. For a 7B-class model at fp16 with 32 layers, 32 heads and head_dim 128, that works out to about 0.5 MB per token, so a 32,000-token conversation claims roughly 15.6 GB for a single sequence. Since a 7B model in fp16 is about 14 GB of weights, an 80 GB card has around 66 GB left and fits only four such conversations; drop the limit to 4,000 tokens and the same card serves thirty-three. A context window is therefore a memory reservation, not a text-length preference.

prompt: What does the KV cache store, and why is caching those particular values valid?
answer_markdown: It stores the key and value vectors computed for each token, at every layer of the model. Caching them is valid because of causal masking: a token's key and value depend only on that token and the ones before it, and nothing later in the sequence can influence them. So token 3's key is identical whether the sequence is 4 tokens long or 4,000 — it is computed once and never changes. Anything that is immutable once computed and needed repeatedly is exactly what a cache is for. Without it, generating token n+1 means re-projecting all n previous tokens into keys and values again, which makes generating n tokens cost roughly n cubed work in the attention path instead of n squared.

prompt: Explain prefill and decode, and why they are bound by different hardware limits.
answer_markdown: Prefill processes your entire prompt in one pass, filling the cache. Every token's key and value can be computed simultaneously because they do not depend on one another, so the GPU runs at full arithmetic throughput — prefill is compute-bound, and its duration sets your time-to-first-token. Decode then generates one token at a time: each step reads the whole KV cache plus every weight in the model, and does a tiny amount of arithmetic with them. The GPU spends its time moving bytes rather than multiplying, so decode is memory-bandwidth-bound and sets your tokens-per-second. This distinction has direct practical consequences: a faster-compute GPU will not speed up decode much, memory bandwidth is the number to look at, and serving stacks batch aggressively because a single read of the weights can serve many sequences at once.

prompt: Why does raising the batch size force you to lower the maximum context length on the same hardware?
answer_markdown: Cache memory is proportional to both sequence length and batch size, and after the model weights are loaded the two compete for one fixed pool of remaining VRAM. There is no way around the multiplication: on a 7B fp16 model with roughly 66 GB free, an 8,000-token context needs about 3.9 GB per sequence, so a batch of 8 consumes over 31 GB, and a batch of 8 at 128,000 tokens would need 500 GB — six of the largest single GPUs available, for eight conversations. Context length times batch size is effectively a fixed budget, which is why self-hosting forces you to configure a maximum model length explicitly, and why increasing concurrency targets always ends in a conversation about shortening prompts.

prompt: What is the real cost of a long system prompt, beyond its token count?
answer_markdown: Two costs that the quoted token count does not reveal. First, the prompt is re-prefilled on every single request unless the serving layer recognises and reuses the identical prefix, so a 2,000-token system prompt is paid for repeatedly across a conversation rather than once. Second, it occupies KV cache space for the entire conversation's lifetime — about 1 GB on a 7B fp16 model — which directly reduces how many concurrent users the same GPU can hold. Prompt caching on the provider side is the lever that addresses the first cost, and `llm-cost-and-latency` covers it from the API-consumer perspective. The general lesson is that prompt length has a memory cost as well as a compute and billing cost.

prompt: The model supports a 128k context window. Should you use it, and what are MQA and GQA for?
answer_markdown: Not by default. Prefill time rises with prompt length so time-to-first-token gets worse; cache memory rises linearly so concurrency drops sharply; and retrieval quality often degrades in the middle of very long contexts, where models attend reliably to the beginning and end but skim the centre. Filling a large window because it exists frequently buys a slower, costlier and less accurate answer than a well-chosen 8k. MQA and GQA attack the memory side of this by shrinking the `heads` term in the cache formula: multi-query attention gives every head its own query but shares one key/value pair across all of them, while grouped-query attention splits heads into groups that each share a K/V pair — 32 heads in 8 groups shrinks the cache fourfold at almost no quality cost, which is why GQA is now the standard choice.
